messages.subject: Re: GWAS-by-subtraction vs. mtCOJO
messages.body_plain:
The potential difference between the standard GWAS-by-subtraction model within Genomic SEM and mtCOJO comes down to how beta_xy is estimated. In the standard GWAS-by-subtraction model the beta_xy is essentially a transformation of the LDSC-estimated genetic covariance matrix among the GWAS phenotypes (x and y) into a structural regression coefficient. For mtCOJO, Zhu et al. write on p. 10 that "we can... estimate beta_xy by GSMR."  However, the software documentation <https://cnsgenomics.com/software/gcta/#mtCOJO> indicates that beta_xy can either be provided by the user (e.g. from a collateral study), estimated with GSMR (i.e. using genome-wide significant variants as instrumental variables for Mendelian Randomization along with removal of HEIDI outliers), or estimated with "genetic correlation analysis" (i.e. the way it is estimated in the standard GWAS-by-subtraction model). My understanding is that the default within mtCOJO is to use GSMR when there are "enough" GWAS significant SNPs, and in the absence of enough GWAS significant SNPs to use genetic correlation analysis. One way to intuit the difference is that the GSMR approach would control for only the portion of shared genetic variance that is causally attributable to x, whereas the GWAS-by-subtraction ("genetic correlation analysis") approach would control for all shared variance.

Apart from potential differences in the the source of beta_xy, my reading of p.10 Zhu et al. is that mtCOJO and the standard GWAS-by-subtraction model are near equivalent. Note that both use the LDSC-derived cross-trait-intercepts to populate elements of the sampling covariance matrix used to compute the SEs of the estimates of SNP effects.

Within Genomic SEM we can fix beta_xy to some value estimated from external data (or simply assumed), or we can expand the GWAS-by-subtraction model within Genomic SEM to include multiple GWAS significant SNPs as instrumental variables for a GSMR type analysis. An advantage of the Genomic SEM approach is that, because the user can specify or modify the model, the assumptions of the model can be changed, relaxed, or tested, and the model can be extended (e.g. to subtract factors rather than individual phenotypes). We do this in great detail in the supplement to Demange.

messages.subject: Interpretation of GWAS-by-Subtraction Effect Estimates
messages.body_plain:
My understanding is that the "sumstats" function transforms coefficients and SEs "such that they are scaled relative to unit-variance scaled phenotypes" (https://github.com/GenomicSEM/GenomicSEM/wiki/4.-Common-Factor-GWAS). When performing a GWAS-by-Subtraction, my understanding is that SNP effects are similarly reported based on unit-variance identification. Can we therefore directly compare the effect estimates for a given SNP on the parent trait and the adjusted trait (either as a difference or ratio)?

For example, given two traits T1 and T2, we could perform GWAS-by-Subtraction to estimate the effect of a SNP on T2adjT1 (T2 independent of T1). For any given SNP we have 1) effect the SNP on T2 scaled to unit variance (from the "sumstats" function), and 2) the effect of the SNP on T2adjT1 scaled to unit variance (from the GWAS-by-Subtraction). Calculating a difference or ratio of these effect estimates seems like it would provide some quantitative assessment of whether the effect of a SNP on T2 is "mediated" by T1. Is this interpretation/intuition correct?

messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of GWAS-by-Subtraction Effect Estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

For GWAS-by-subtraction with unit-scaled factors and free loadings, the SNP effects actually get rescaled by the loadings. This is because this parameterization scales the genetic variance, rather than the phenotypic variance, of the factor to 1.0, whereas the sumstats function scales the SNP effects relative to unit-scaled phenotypes (this is exactly what we typically want because that's the scale that heritability is on). You could parameterize the GWAS-by-subtraction model such that the variances of the factors are free and the loadings are fixed to 1.0 (keep the cross loading of EA on Cog free), which would be an equivalent model but put the SNP effects on the same scale as those from the sumstats function. The rGs, top hits, mean chi sq, etc.. will all be the same as the original parameterization but the scale will just be changed for the SNP betas.

You'll be able to confirm whether or not the betas are indeed on the same scale as those from sumstats by comparing the SNP betas for the Cog factor from the GWAS-by-subtraction model to those for Cognitive Performance from the sumstats function. Cog and cognitive performance are the same in this model, since nothing is being subtracted from Cognitive Performance when forming the Cog factor, so the Z statistics should match regardless, but the betas will be rescaled depending on your parameterization.

Hope that helps,

Elliot

Hope it's okay that I jump on this thread - I have similar questions.

I ran a common factor model using the userGWAS function for reasons similar to Dan's. Some SNPs also still generated negative variance warnings (also, like Dan, this was a small proportion of the output).

For the independent pathways model, I did:

PHENO2 ~~ b*PHENO2

PHENO3 ~~ c* PHENO3

PHENO1 ~ SNP
PHENO2 ~ SNP

indep <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput, SNPs = split_sumstats, model = mod_indep, parallel = T, cores = 6, sub = c("PHENO1~SNP", "PHENO2~SNP", "PHENO3~SNP"))

Thanks so much,

Sarah

Responding to both Sarah and Dan here:

Dan, my guess is you have at least one variable that has a residual variance in the model without individual SNPs that is close enough to 0 that in the model with the SNPs that in some rare cases you end up with the negative variance warnings you are highlighting. If it's a really small proportion of your SNPs, then you could consider just excluding them. My honest response is I could see going either way as far as whether you run them through userGWAS with the constraints or just drop them, but would probably go with the userGWAS option myself.

Sarah, you are correct that just taking the chisq on the common pathways model for a 3 df factor is equal to the Q_SNP index. When you say all of the chi-square values are significant are you using 5e-8 as the significance threshold?

-Andrew

Hi Sarah,

Thanks for sending along the code and data files! I'm just replying here so others who run into this issue can see the response and also because there may be varying opinions out there on this one so if anyone else on the Genomic SEM team or otherwise wants to weigh in please feel free.

It looks like the issue is that you are still getting a fair amount of misfit for the part of the model that should not be contributing to overall mode chi-square. More specifically, the constraint on the residual variance for Phenotype 2 is causing misfit for that part of the matrix, and you can see that the model chi-square drops to nonsignificant across the example SNPs you sent if you remove the constraints on the residual variance. This hasn't come up before because for models with multiple factors or with a single factor with > 3 indicators, Q_SNP is still calculated by comparing the model chi-square estimates across the common and independent pathways models and the chi-square contribution for misfit caused due to constraints on the residual variances simply cancels out across those comparisons. However, as you correctly pointed out in your earlier question, for a 3 indicator you should in theory just be able to run the common pathways model since the independent pathways model is fully saturated, but that has yielded the issue you ran into where that misfit doesn't cancel out and you get the highly significant model chi-square for all SNPs. So that's why the issue is arising and I can see a couple of options in this instance:

1. You could remove the constraints on the residual variances and note that this is an interpretive limitation of the model that it produces the negative residual

2. You could fix the residual variance to 0 to mirror what the constraint is effectively doing and so that the independent pathways model is no longer fully saturated and you can then do the model chi-square comparison such that misfit due to Phenotype_2 cancels out across the models as would typically happen in these sorts of instances. Example code for what I'm suggesting here is below:

common_mod <- 'F1 =~ PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3
PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1
a > 0.001
PHENO2 ~~ 0*PHENO2
PHENO3 ~~ c*PHENO3
c > 0.001
F1~SNP'

common_factor <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput_COG_v2, SNPs = sumstats_5SNPs,sub=c("F1~SNP"), model = common_mod, parallel = F)

ind_mod <- 'F1 =~ PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3
PHENO1 ~~ a*PHENO1
a > 0.001
PHENO2 ~~ 0*PHENO2
PHENO3 ~~ c*PHENO3
c > 0.001
PHENO1 + PHENO2 + PHENO3~SNP'

ind_factor <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput_COG_v2, SNPs = sumstats_5SNPs, sub="PHENO1~SNP",model = ind_mod, parallel = F)

Q_SNP<-pchisq(common_factor[[1]]$chisq-ind_factor[[1]]$chisq,common_factor[[1]]$chisq_df-ind_factor[[1]]$chisq_df,lower.tail=FALSE)

3. You can revisit the choice of traits included in your model and try to find an additional trait or traits to include in your model. If you look at the genetic correlation matrix across your traits, Pheno 2 correlates at .7 across the other two traits, while Pheno1 and Pheno3 correlate at .3. It makes sense, given the observed data, that you then end up with model estimates where it is trying to push the factor loading for Pheno2 up to a point where the residual variance goes negative since it correlates so much stronger with the other traits. I know this is next to impossible to do as for as a prior trait selection, but if you had some sense of other traits that you could include that correlate more strongly with Pheno 1 or 3, or correlate moderate to strong with all three phenotypes, that would help balance out the "centrality" of Pheno2 in your factor.

Best,
  Andrew

Hi Sarah,

Just to be clear, option 2 requires doing the model comparison across the common and independent pathways model since the independent pathways model is no longer fully saturated. Two points to consider in response to your question:

1. Whether filtering on Q is the appropriate approach for downstream analysis on the factor depends somewhat on the analysis you want to do. For example, if you are examining functional enrichment, I would recommend estimating that directly within the model using Stratified Genomic SEM. I know for others a research question of interest is how the factor correlates with other external traits. In that case, I would estimate the LDSC object using that external trait and estimate the genetic correlations within the model itself since those will be unbiased by heterogeneity in SNP-level signal. That said, if your planned follow-up analyses falls outside of these two instances then yes filtering on Q_SNP would be the way to go.

2. If you are filtering out Q_SNPs for downstream analyses on the multivariate GWAS summary statistics for a factor you might consider also filtering out SNPs in LD with the signifiant Q_hits at some R^2 threshold (e.g., > 0.6).

Best,
  Andrew
